name: Zenoh (throughput/latency study vs MQTT, Kafka, DDS)
workload: Pub/sub throughput (msg/s and bit/s) and ping-pong latency across payload sizes 8B-512MiB on single-machine and multi-machine (100GbE) setups, comparing Zenoh 0.7.0-rc, Mosquitto MQTT 2.0.15, Kafka broker 3.2.1 (rdkafka client), and Eclipse Cyclone DDS.
claimed_speedup: Zenoh peer-mode ~60-65x Kafka msg/s and ~55-65x Kafka bit/s at 8B payload (single- and multi-machine); ~12x Kafka at 32KiB payload; Kafka saturates at ~53-62K msg/s / 3-5 Gbps vs Zenoh's >4M msg/s / up to 67 Gbps
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X @ fixed 4.0 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS; multi-machine scenario used 100 Gb Ethernet
tradeoffs: Zenoh is a decentralized pub/sub protocol (no broker required in peer mode), different architecture/consistency model than Kafka's replicated commit log; Kafka bindings used (rdkafka) failed above 1MB messages, capping Kafka's tested range and possibly disadvantaging it at large payloads
caveats: Authors are Zenoh/Zettascale-affiliated (first-party for the winning system), so treat as a vendor-run comparison though methodology, code, and hardware are public; Kafka tuned per online docs rather than by Kafka experts; arXiv preprint, not confirmed peer-reviewed; is_evidence_for_known applies since eclipse-zenoh/zenoh is already catalogued

name: SMF write-ahead-log (Seastar Message Fabric)
workload: Write 100M records (100-byte and 8196-message batches) to a Seastar-based O_DIRECT/XFS/NVMe write-ahead log vs Apache Kafka 2.11-1.0 (lz4 compression, 32 partitions) on the same NVMe/XFS/kernel-4.14 host; measured end-to-end and server-observed tail latency.
claimed_speedup: 48x lower P-max/tail latency than Apache Kafka (Kafka slowest 1618ms vs SMF slowest 34ms) after a performance-debugging pass that started 1.3x slower than Kafka
hardware: NVMe + XFS, Linux kernel 4.14.16-300.fc27.x86_64; exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Built on Seastar's thread-per-core model with O_DIRECT/AIO; single-node write-ahead-log component, not a full distributed broker with replication/consumer-group semantics like Kafka; blog author is the project's creator (later founded Redpanda, which reuses this storage-engine lineage and is already catalogued)
caveats: First-party blog post by the project author; exact CPU model, compiler, and flags not stated; localhost-only test (author notes this omits network-rack latency); GitHub SPDX shows NOASSERTION but LICENSE file confirms Apache-2.0; repo itself is abandoned (no commits >3 years)
found_via: HN Algolia query 'faster than Kafka' -> alexgallego.org blog post

name: Fluvio
workload: Produce 200,000 records at 5120 bytes each via kafka-producer-perf-test.sh vs `fluvio benchmark producer`, run on both a MacBook Pro M1 Max (32GB RAM) and an AWS EC2 c7g.xlarge (Graviton3, 4 vCPU/8GB RAM); measured records/sec, MB/sec throughput, and P99 latency.
claimed_speedup: 1.5x throughput and 20-38x lower P99 latency than Kafka; e.g. on M1 Max: 76,923 rec/s / 394.6 MB/s / 5.8ms P99 (Fluvio) vs 49,346 rec/s / 240.95 MB/s / 132ms P99 (Kafka); on EC2 c7g.xlarge: 37,195 rec/s / 190.8 MB/s / 10.8ms P99 (Fluvio) vs 26,780 rec/s / 130.77 MB/s / 419ms P99 (Kafka)
hardware: MacBook Pro 18 (Apple M1 Max, 10-core, 32GB RAM); AWS EC2 c7g.xlarge (AWS Graviton3 ARM64, 4 vCPU, 8GB RAM, EBS)
tradeoffs: Fluvio is a Rust/WebAssembly streaming engine following Kafka's conceptual model but a different implementation and ecosystem (no JVM/GC pause overhead); default-config comparison, both systems left largely untuned; Kafka's JVM warm-up period included in results, which understates Kafka's steady-state numbers somewhat
caveats: First-party vendor (InfinyOn, makers of Fluvio) blog post; exact Kafka and Fluvio versions, compiler flags, and JVM tuning not stated; only default configs tested, no repeated-run error bars given; benchmark harness commands shown but not a public reproducible benchmark repo/CI artifact
found_via: HN Algolia query 'faster than Kafka' -> Show HN: Fluvio 38.8x faster than Kafka

name: Walrus (embedded log/WAL storage engine)
workload: 10-thread sustained write benchmark (pwrite()-based legacy append path, no io_uring batching) against a single Apache Kafka broker (no replication, no network hop, acks=all, enable.idempotence=true) and RocksDB's WAL, on Linux, measuring writes/sec and MB/s for both unsynced and fsync'd ('synced') writes.
claimed_speedup: Unsynced: Walrus avg 1,205,762 writes/s (876.22 MB/s) vs Kafka avg 1,112,120 writes/s (808.33 MB/s), ~8% higher; max 1,593,984 vs 1,424,073 writes/s. Synced/fsync'd writes: roughly tied (Walrus 4,980 vs Kafka 4,921 writes/s avg), with RocksDB slightly ahead of both at 5,222 writes/s avg
hardware: Linux; exact CPU model, RAM, and storage device not stated in the post (benchmark code public at github.com/nubskr/walrus/tree/master/benchmarks, including a Kafka-producer Java harness)
tradeoffs: Single-node, embedded-in-process engine (no replication/partitioning at the time of this benchmark; distributed mode added later); benchmarked against a single Kafka broker with no replication or network hop, i.e. a best-case setup for Kafka rather than a real cluster; margin over Kafka is modest (~8% unsynced, roughly tied when fsync'd) rather than a large multiple
caveats: First-party benchmark by the project's sole author; CPU model, RAM, and disk hardware not stated in either release post, so it falls short of Tier A despite having public benchmark code and stated OS/config; numbers are close enough (within noise) for synced writes that the throughput win is really only in the unsynced/no-fsync configuration
found_via: HN Algolia query 'outperforms Kafka' -> Show HN item 45654988 (Walrus) -> nubskr.com v0.2.0 blog post
